title: Brokered Burst Custodian & Tenant Shed Playbook (PRD Draft)
body:
Summary:

This is a working PRD describing the Brokered Burst Custodian concept for Dedicated capacity. The idea: introduce a lightweight broker layer that acts as a custodial marketplace for short-lived burst capacity, combined with a tenant-shed protocol that gracefully reduces lower-priority tenant load when contention threatens SLOs. Goal is to preserve latency SLOs for high-priority tenants, provide predictable economic controls for burst consumers, and offer operational clarity for SREs.

Why this exists (motivation):
- We see frequent short-duration spikes where isolated tenants request > reserved throughput. Current approaches (hard throttles, wholesale preemption) are blunt and either overpenalize customers or risk SLO violations.
- Customers want predictable economics for bursts (pay-for-burst) and more granular controls than coarse soft-quota.
- Operators need observable, reversible mechanisms for surge events that don't require manual intervention.

Core thesis:
Broker + custody model provides:
- A negotiable, time-bounded burst currency (credits) that can be reserved or on-demand borrowed.
- A custody pool that temporarily maps ephemeral GPU slots to tenants with enforced tenant-level micro-isolation.
- A staged tenant-shed protocol that lowers fidelity/throughput for selected tenants rather than full eviction.

Scope (this draft):
- Functional design for Broker API, Custody Pool semantics, and Tenant Shed protocol.
- Autoscaling interactions (how Dedicated autoscaler cooperates with broker).
- Tenant billing/credit lifecycle for burst consumption.
- Operator runbook for surge events and recovery.
- Monitoring and telemetry contract.

Out of scope (for now):
- On-prem install packaging and HSM integration for billing.
- Deep kernel/runtime changes to model executor (will be handled by serving-runtime team).

User stories / personas:
- Platform Engineer (SRE): "When a cross-tenant surge happens, I want the system to automatically route burst traffic to a custody pool and enforce latency SLOs without manual shard reconfiguration."
- Product/Customer (mid-market team): "I want to allow my app to burst above reserved capacity up to X units/hour with explicit cost predictability and graceful degradation if bursts exceed allowances."
- Solutions Engineer: "I need a clear step-by-step to explain to enterprise customers how bursts are billed and what their app will experience if shed."

Requirements (must-have):
1) Broker API: endpoints for reserve_burst, borrow_burst, repay_burst, preflight (estimate cost/latency impact), and query_credit_balance.
2) Custody Pool: ephemeral assignment unit (slot) with metadata (tenant_id, duration, CPU/GPU type, quantization_profile).
3) Tenant Shed Protocol: staged fidelity levels (full, reduced-fidelity, batched, queueing, soft-throttle) and selection heuristics.
4) Autoscaler cooperation: broker insights should inform predictive warm-pool allocation; autoscaler must be able to provision custody pool capacity ahead of expected bursts.
5) Observable economics: per-tenant burst units consumed, cost per unit, and bucket balance.
6) SLO guarantees: broker must not increase p99 latency for protected tenants beyond configured hedges.

Non-functional requirements:
- Latency overhead of broker decision path < 5ms median for admission checks when custody pool available.
- Custody slots should be reclaimable with graceful timeout signaling (e.g., 5–30s).
- Security: broker communication must be authenticated and auditable.

Proposal (high-level design):
1) Broker service (stateless front-end + small state store):
   - Accepts reserve/borrow requests. Maintains per-tenant credit ledger (time-decayed credit buckets), and global custody inventory view.
   - Implements pricing model: base price per slot-second plus dynamic surge multiplier (0–3x) tied to global utilization and SLO pressure.

2) Custody pool manager:
   - Runs in Dedicated control plane. Maintains a pool of prewarmed fidelity-agnostic slots (hot standbys). Slots have labels (gpu-class, seq-len-opt).
   - When broker grants a custody ticket, the scheduler pins a slot to tenant and injects routing keys and KV separation. KV caches for the tenant are isolated for the ticket duration (eviction policy in notes below).

3) Tenant shed protocol (staged):
   - Stage 0: No action (within reservation).
   - Stage 1: Soft batching (combine short requests into micro-batches for same tenant).
   - Stage 2: Reduced-fidelity model variant (less compute) if available.
   - Stage 3: Queueing gate with progressive delay and SLA notice header returned to client.
   - Stage 4: Final soft-throttle (reject new requests above configured throughput).
   - Selection policy: choose tenants with lowest SLA weight and highest elasticity score; avoid shedding customers currently in a canary rollout or flagged as high-priority.

APIs (sketch):
- POST /broker/reserve_burst {tenant_id, seconds, slot_type, max_cost} -> {ticket_id, estimated_cost, start_time, expiry}
- POST /broker/borrow_burst {tenant_id, desired_slots, max_latency_penalty} -> {ticket_id, assigned_slots, surge_price_mult}
- POST /broker/repay_burst {ticket_id} -> {final_cost}
- GET /broker/credit_balance?tenant_id= -> {credits_available, decay_rate, outstanding_tickets}
- GET /broker/preflight?tenant_id=&expected_qps=&seq_len= -> {expected_cost, p50/p95/p99_estimate}

Billing model (concept):
- Tenants can pre-purchase burst credits (discounted) or take on-demand bursts at market rate.
- Credits are consumed per slot-second and rounded to nearest second. Refunds for early release apply at 80% of unit price if release > 10s early.
- Overspend alerts: agents warn at 70%, 90% of monthly burst budget.

Autoscaler interactions:
- Broker exposes horizon signals to autoscaler: anticipated burst window, ticket backlog length, and target pool size.
- Autoscaler maintains two waterlines: baseline reserved capacity (unchanged) and broker-backed hot pool target (dynamic).
- Warmup: for GPU-heavy models, autoscaler must prewarm shards N minutes before predicted burst; broker provides predictive demand windows based on historical tenant usage.

Isolation semantics and KV cache handling: 
- Custody tickets create a soft namespace boundary. KV cache warmness is not transferred between tenants; we maintain per-tenant cached prefixes in a short-lived cache store attached to ticket. On ticket assignment, we allow a prefetch window to load likely prefixes (best-effort).
- Eviction: when ticket ends, attached cached prefixes are TTL'd to 1 minute and then evicted to avoid noisy neighbor privacy leakage and memory creep.

Operational playbook (brief):
- Surge detection: system triggers when global burst utilization > 70% for > 30s. Broker auto-allocates custody tickets until pool drained.
- If SLO pressure (p99 > target) on protected tenants: escalate to tenant-shed stage 2 for opportunistic tenants and raise surge price multiplier.
- Manual intervention: SRE can mark a tenant as "protect" which removes them from shedding selection for 24h.
- Post-mortem: every surge event must include ticket_id list, shedding timeline, and cost impact; attach to JIRA with tag DEDICATED-SURGE.

Monitoring / telemetry contract:
- Per-ticket metrics: created_at, start_at, end_at, tenant_id, assigned_slots, surrogate_price, final_cost.
- Global metrics: custody_pool_utilization, ticket_backlog, surge_price_index, p99_protected_tenants, shed_rate_by_tenant.
- Alerts:
   - P0: protected_tenant_p99 > SLO for > 2m -> page on-call SRE
   - P1: custody_pool_utilization > 95% and ticket_backlog > 20 -> notify on-call
   - P2: repeated shedding for same tenant > 3 times/day -> product review

Testing & rollout plan (phased):
- Stage A (lab): unit tests for broker logic, sim harness to model 100 tenants with spikes; failover tests where autoscaler cannot provision.
- Stage B (canary): enable broker for 3 non-critical tenants in us-west1 with strict caps; monitor economics and latency.
- Stage C (beta): expand to 20 tenants with mixed fidelity models and run for a month.
- Stage D (GA): open to all tenants with UI in Console for purchasing credits and telemetry.

Metrics for success:
- Reduce urgent manual eviction incidents by 60% in first 3 months post-GA.
- Keep p99 latency for protected tenants within 1.2x baseline during 95% of surge windows.
- Achieve > 80% predictability of burst billing (preflight estimate within ±20% of final cost).

Failure modes & mitigations:
- Broker outage: fallback is immediate soft-throttle to reserved capacity; tickets in flight are marked for graceful expiration. Mitigation: broker is deployed multi-region and stores ledger in replicated service.
- Abuse (cost escalation): enforce per-tenant spend caps and automatic suspend on policy violation.
- Privacy leakage via caches: enforce strict eviction and per-tenant encryption keys for KV cache.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Pricing: should we lock surge multiplier to a 24h rolling average or allow real-time spikes? Pros/cons listed below.
- Prewarming cost model: who absorbs warmup cost if prewarmed pool is idle? Options: platform subsidy, tenant prepaid warmup credit, or dynamic bill-back.
- Should custody tickets support fractional GPU shares (vGPU)? Feasible but complex for isolation.
- Need input from serving-runtime on fast reclaim strategies and tenant cache snapshotting.

Appendix (notes to self):
- Experiment idea: dynamic hedging where tenants can opt into "lossy-hedge" to promise lower-quality outputs during surge for lower burst pricing. Add UX knob in Console.
- Related artifacts: link to cost-simulator in repo, and to dedicated autoscaler telem spec.

Immediate next steps:
1) Sync with serving-runtime and autoscaler owners (Meera + Liam) for feasibility.
2) Prototype broker preflight API in a test harness and run synthetic spikes.
3) Draft Console UX flows for credit purchase, ticket history, and shed notifications.

Notes: rough sketch — many heuristics intentionally underspecified. This doc is meant as a collaborative starting point for product/engineers/SRE to iterate.

-- end of draft --
